title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is led by mounting pressure on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after reports of a second affair, and by Democrat Scott Colom's narrow Senate win in Mississippi. It also covers a White House warning to incoming Democratic investigators, Spain's first general strike in 14 years, a South Carolina infant rescued after being buried alive, Toyota's US-built kei truck, and several regional stories from Charlotte and Korea.

stories.headline: Nvidia shares fall as reports say board weighs removing CEO Jensen Huang after second alleged affair
stories.summary: The New York Times reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, 63, had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. This follows Huang's admission days earlier of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials reportedly believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence. The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board is preparing to remove Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday. Nvidia has launched an independent investigation and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. House Republicans have sought a closed-door briefing from Huang, and the FBI is looking into the matter, according to President Trump.
key_facts: Nvidia stock fell more than 7% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the second report (The Verge).
Nvidia lost more than $427 billion in market value in the first two trading sessions after Huang's disclosure (Fox Business).
Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer called for Huang to resign; House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast threatened a subpoena if Huang did not respond by the end of Wednesday.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips over about two years and denies helping Chinese firms obtain restricted chips.
Baird downgraded Nvidia to neutral; Morgan Stanley and Bank of America removed it from their top-pick lists.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera focused on national security, asking what Chinese intelligence might have learned and quoting lawmakers and experts on chip export controls and Megaspeed. It also noted Trump's defense of Huang as an 'honourable guy.' The Verge focused on the board's reported plan to fire Huang, details of the alleged Powell relationship, and Huang's earlier hiring of a crisis-communications firm known for sex scandals.

Axios framed the story around market reaction and broader stakes, calling Huang arguably the world's most powerful CEO with no obvious successor. The Hill profiled Alice Huang and the allegations against her.

Fox Business emphasised Wall Street fallout, including analyst downgrades and lost market value, alongside the WSJ report on Huang's possible removal. Washington Examiner briefly reported the ouster preparations, centring on the alleged Chinese spy.

disputed: Whether Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence operative is alleged by US officials, according to the Times, but unproven.
Whether any secrets were compromised: Nvidia says it has no reason to believe so, while experts and lawmakers question this.
The alleged Powell relationship rests on unnamed sources; the Times has not seen the hotel video they describe.
Whether the board will actually remove Huang had not been confirmed; Nvidia did not comment.
stories.why: Nvidia is central to the AI industry and US-China chip policy, so leadership turmoil and espionage questions there have market and national-security consequences.

stories.headline: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi
stories.summary: The AP projected that Democrat Scott Colom unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi after more than a week of counting, by roughly half a percentage point. Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hyde-Smith conceded in a video, saying she respected voters' decision. Democrats celebrated the win as part of midterm gains that gave them control of both chambers of Congress.
key_facts: Colom won 49.19% to Hyde-Smith's 48.71%, per the AP as cited by the Daily Caller.
Trump won Mississippi with 60.9% in 2024; Hyde-Smith won in 2020 with 54.1%.
Daily Caller reports Democrats now hold 55 Senate seats, with Alaska's race still uncalled.
Colom's campaign ran a viral ad over Hyde-Smith's 'so many proteins to choose from' remark on beef prices.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian gave detailed, celebratory coverage of Colom's victory rally at Tougaloo College, emphasising historical significance, civil-rights-era attendees, prayer and his family's history. PBS briefly noted the result in a news roundup.
Axios called it a 'stunning' upset and part of a 'historic blue wave,' highlighting the racial milestone. The Hill focused on Democrats rallying around the win, quoting Bill Clinton.

Daily Caller reported the result straightforwardly with vote shares and Hyde-Smith's concession, and linked to pieces suggesting Democrats lack a mandate. Washington Examiner called it one of the biggest upsets of the midterms, citing Trump's 2024 margin in the state.

disputed: Outlets differ on the last time Mississippi elected a Democratic senator: Axios says since 1982, while Daily Caller says Colom is the first Democrat to represent the state since 1989.
Framing of the milestone differs: Axios says first Black senator since Reconstruction; The Guardian says first elected since 1874.
stories.why: A Democratic Senate win in a deeply Republican state signals the scale of the midterm shift and affects the size of the incoming Senate majority.

stories.headline: White House letter warns Democrats' planned investigations 'may cross the line into blatant criminality'
stories.summary: White House counsel William Scharf sent a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight chair, warning that Democrats' planned probes of the administration could exceed constitutional limits and 'may cross the line into blatant criminality.' The letter cited Democratic statements such as Garcia's 'lawyer up' post and pledges to issue many subpoenas. Garcia responded that Trump appears to have 'something to hide' and that Congress will not be deterred. The exchange comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress on January 3, and amid a wave of senior Justice Department resignations.
key_facts: The letter was sent Monday and released publicly Wednesday.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that Democrats' statements were 'extortion at the highest level'; Attorney General Todd Blanche agreed they could be crimes.
Garcia said Congress's authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, 'not from the permission of the White House.'
Departing DOJ officials include Harmeet Dhillon, Brett Shumate and John Eisenberg (PBS).

perspectives.framing: PBS described the letter as a threat and interviewed NYT reporter Devlin Barrett, who called it legally weak but politically significant and linked it to DOJ resignations. Al Jazeera and The Guardian gave substantial space to both the letter's text and Garcia's rebuttal, with The Guardian adding context on corruption as a midterm issue.
The Hill framed the letter as the administration floating the idea of investigating the investigators, part of an aggressive stance toward oversight.

Reason (lean-right) was critical of the White House, arguing that Democrats' remarks were ordinary political rhetoric and protected speech, and noting that neither Trump nor Blanche explained what crime was involved. It quoted Politico calling the letter a departure from precedent.

disputed: The letter does not say what action the White House might take if Democrats proceed.
Whether congressional oversight statements could be criminal is disputed; the administration has not set out a legal theory.
Reasons for the DOJ resignations are not fully clear; Barrett noted post-election departures are not unusual.
stories.why: The clash previews a likely legal and political fight over congressional subpoenas and executive-branch accountability once the new Congress is seated.

stories.headline: South Carolina father charged with attempted murder after infant found buried alive
stories.summary: An 11-month-old boy, Koah, was found alive Tuesday in a buried dog crate in woods near his grandfather's home in Lexington County, South Carolina, after a search by about 100 first responders. Searchers spotted freshly disturbed soil and heard him crying. His father, 25-year-old Michael Comer, now faces charges including attempted murder, and the sheriff's office directly accused him of burying the child alive. The child has left the hospital and is expected to recover fully; Comer has a bond hearing Thursday.
key_facts: Comer is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.
Sheriff Jay Koon said a towel around the crate likely created an air pocket; the baby was believed buried about 24 hours.
Comer was arrested Monday night hiding in an outbuilding, without the child.
Comer was placed on probation in October after a guilty plea and had earlier domestic violence arrests.

perspectives.framing: PBS ran the AP report, focusing on the rescue, the sheriff's quotes and family members' accounts, including that Comer had talked of taking the baby to New York.

WBTV gave the most detail, including the new charges, a timeline and Comer's criminal history. BBC and WCNC centred on the rescue and the sheriff's description, with the BBC quoting Comer's mother saying she 'never expected this.'

disputed: The child's surname is spelled 'Sharp' by most outlets and 'Sharpe' by the BBC.
Comer's motive has not been established, and it was unclear whether he had a lawyer.
stories.why: The case raises questions about child safety where there is prior domestic violence, and it now moves to court.

stories.headline: Toyota revives Scion brand with US-built kei truck capped at 25 mph
stories.summary: Toyota announced it is bringing back the Scion brand as 'Scion by Toyota,' an experimental line whose first vehicle, the KEI-01, is a Japanese-style kei truck to be built in Indiana. The truck will be certified as a federal low-speed vehicle, limiting top speed to 25 mph. Outlets linked the move to President Trump's stated interest last year in allowing kei vehicles in the US. It is due in the second half of 2027; pricing has not been announced.
key_facts: The KEI-01 has a 660cc three-cylinder engine, CVT and on-demand four-wheel drive.
Toyota is investing $34 million in its Princeton, Indiana plant.
Washington Examiner reports the equivalent Japanese model can reach 87 mph.
More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported to the US since 2020 (The Verge).

perspectives.framing: The Verge gave a detailed, generally positive product rundown, emphasising utility and fleet use while noting the cheap interior and speed cap.
Ars Technica set the news in a policy context, arguing that US fuel-economy rules encouraged large SUVs and noting that the DOT has said little about Trump's kei push.
Washington Examiner highlighted Trump's admiration for kei trucks and stressed the 'catch' of the 25 mph limit compared with the Japanese version.

disputed: Price and trim levels are not yet disclosed.
It is unclear what regulatory changes, if any, the DOT has made on kei vehicles.
stories.why: It tests whether Americans will buy very small utility vehicles, and how far federal rules will bend to allow them.

stories.headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing costs ahead of snap election
stories.summary: Millions of workers in Spain joined a 24-hour general strike Wednesday over housing shortages, rents and living costs, followed by mass evening marches in Madrid and Barcelona. Most protests were peaceful, but small groups clashed with police in Barcelona, burning bins, smashing shop windows and firing fireworks; more than 50 people were arrested nationwide. The strike comes before a November 29 snap election that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called after parliament blocked his housing reforms. The conservative People's Party and far-right Vox called it an 'election strike' meant to help the government, and polls point to a possible right-wing majority.
key_facts: Officials estimated 120,000 marched in Madrid; Barcelona police estimated 55,000, while organisers claimed 400,000.
Tenants' groups said about 4 million people took part by midday.
The Bank of Spain estimates a shortage of about 750,000 homes, potentially rising to over 1 million.
The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who died weeks later, became a symbol of the crisis.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian emphasised scale and participation figures, quoted tenants' union activists and older protesters worried for their children, and framed the election as one where the far right could gain power. Al Jazeera's short piece led with violence in Barcelona and the union turnout claim.

DW, BBC and CNBC combined turnout, housing data and the Barcelona clashes, and set out the political dimension, quoting both union leaders and PP accusations of an 'election strike.' The BBC also quoted a protester describing the march as mostly peaceful and 'joyful.'

disputed: Turnout figures vary widely between police and organisers.
Who called the strike: The Guardian says tenants' associations first called it with unions later backing it; BBC and CNBC say the main unions called it.
Government stance: DW says the government supported the strike, while CNBC says it did not officially endorse it.
Pickets said police used pepper spray at Mercamadrid, sending at least 13 people for medical attention; this is a protester account.
stories.why: Housing affordability is reshaping Spain's election, which could bring a change of government in one of Europe's largest economies.

stories.headline: Charlotte police find car but not driver after fatal hit-and-run
stories.summary: A pedestrian, 43-year-old Niceforo Garcia-Rufino, was struck and killed Tuesday night near Nations Ford Road and East Arrowood Road in Charlotte. Police say the driver of a red Mercedes-Benz was speeding and fled; the car has been found but the driver has not. City Council member Joi Mayo proposed an initiative to help residents report broken streetlights. Police are asking witnesses to contact investigators.
key_facts: The crash happened around 8:50 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10.
Police say the victim was crossing outside a marked crosswalk.
Duke Energy maintains Charlotte's streetlights and runs an outage-reporting site.

perspectives.framing: All four local outlets reported the police search; WBTV added the streetlight proposal, residents' safety concerns and a recent string of pedestrian deaths.

disputed: The driver's identity is unknown.
Whether lighting played a role is not established; WBTV noted at least a dozen streetlights visible from the intersection.
stories.why: It adds to a series of pedestrian deaths in the Charlotte area and to local debate over road safety.

stories.headline: Former FBI agents say Nvidia case shows espionage risks for tech executives
stories.summary: Former FBI agents commented on the alleged Chinese spy affair involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Tracy Walder said Huang 'should have known better' and should have had advisers warning him. Mark Trott described Silicon Valley as 'a center for espionage' and said foreign intelligence officers target executives' vulnerabilities to obtain technology and influence policy.
key_facts: Huang admitted the affair and apologised Sunday; Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation.
The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

perspectives.framing: The Hill focused on Walder's view that Huang's judgement was at fault and that his advisers failed him.

Fox Business used Trott's interview to frame the case as part of a broader espionage threat to Silicon Valley, with practical advice for executives. It also linked to items on China denying the plot and a short seller who had flagged the ties.

disputed: China denies any spy plot and calls the allegations a 'smear,' according to a Fox Business headline.
stories.why: The case is drawing attention to foreign intelligence targeting of people with access to sensitive technology.

stories.headline: K-pop group Cortis passes 1.5 billion Spotify streams
stories.summary: BigHit Music said K-pop boy band Cortis has passed 1.5 billion cumulative Spotify streams 15 months after debuting. Its most-streamed song, 'RedRed,' has about 276 million streams. The agency says the group reached the mark faster than other recent boy-band debuts.
key_facts: Yonhap reports nearly 1.6 billion streams as of Tuesday, about 1.2 billion of them this year.
The second EP, 'Greengreen,' had sold more than 4.4 million copies as of October (Korea Herald).

perspectives.framing: Both Korean outlets relayed the agency's announcement and milestone claims.

disputed: The comparison group differs: Yonhap says boy bands that debuted in the past five years, while the Korea Herald says the past year.
Release timing differs: Yonhap says 'RedRed' came out in April, while the Herald says its EP came out in May.
stories.why: It reflects the commercial reach of newer K-pop acts on global streaming.

stories.headline: South Korea's Lee to attend ASEAN and APEC summits; Seoul sees slim chance of North Korea–US talks
stories.summary: President Lee Jae Myung will attend the ASEAN summit in Manila on Monday and Tuesday, then the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday and Thursday. He plans to discuss critical minerals, transnational crime and food security, and to seek support for Seoul's North Korea policy. A presidential official said North Korea is unlikely to attend APEC and the chance of North Korea–US talks there is low. The official said a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC 'cannot be ruled out.'
key_facts: Lee attends a welcome dinner hosted by Xi Jinping on Wednesday.
Trump said a possible meeting with Xi and Putin could cover denuclearization and ending the war in Iran.
South Korea's Cabinet approved a bill to extend its Cheonghae anti-piracy unit's operations toward the Strait of Hormuz, pending parliamentary consent.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap focused on Lee's itinerary and goals; the Korea Herald led with the low likelihood of North Korea–US talks and the Hormuz deployment.

disputed: Whether a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting or any Trump-Kim contact will happen remains speculative.
stories.why: The summits could shape regional diplomacy on North Korea, trade and security.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: None of this edition's articles address AI regulation in the US or EU. The Nvidia coverage mentions US chip export restrictions to China but no new regulatory action.
